ukmt-jmc-2023-01.title: Check by adding
ukmt-jmc-2023-01.body:
Add each option to $2023$ and look for $3202$: $2023+1179 = 3202$. (Also, only C ends in the right digit: the answer must end in $2-3 \to 9$.)

**Answer: (C) 1179**

ukmt-jmc-2023-02.title: Test each option
ukmt-jmc-2023-02.body:
The options are the numbers $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$. Since $30 = 1\times30 = 2\times15 = 3\times10 = 5\times6$, the numbers $1, 2, 3, 5$ are factors, but $4$ is not ($30\div4 = 7.5$). So four of them are factors.

**Answer: (D) 4**

ukmt-jmc-2023-02.title: Use the prime factorisation
ukmt-jmc-2023-02.body:
$30 = 2\times3\times5$ has no factor $2\times2$, so $4$ is not a factor; every other option ($1$ and the primes $2, 3, 5$) divides $30$. That makes $4$ factors.

**Answer: (D) 4**

ukmt-jmc-2023-03.title: Add, then simplify
ukmt-jmc-2023-03.body:
Top: $1+2+3+4+5 = 15$. Bottom: $6+7+8+9+10 = 40$. So the fraction is $\frac{15}{40} = \frac38$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac38$**

ukmt-jmc-2023-03.title: Use the middle numbers
ukmt-jmc-2023-03.body:
Each sum of five consecutive numbers is $5$ times its middle number: $5\times3 = 15$ and $5\times8 = 40$. So the fraction is $\frac{5\times3}{5\times8} = \frac38$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac38$**

ukmt-jmc-2023-04.title: Test from the largest
ukmt-jmc-2023-04.body:
We are told one of the options is the answer, so test them from the largest down.
- $96$: product $9\times6 = 54$, and $96$ is not divisible by $54$.
- $72$: product $7\times2 = 14$, and $72$ is not divisible by $14$.
- $36$: product $3\times6 = 18$, and $36 = 2\times18$. Yes!

So $36$ is the largest of the options that works, and therefore it is the number.

**Answer: (C) 36**

ukmt-jmc-2023-04.title: Check the numbers above 36
ukmt-jmc-2023-04.body:
A number $\overline{ab}$ divisible by $a\times b$ must be divisible by its units digit $b$, and also by $a$. Checking every two-digit number from $37$ to $99$ in this way (a quick computer search confirms it) shows none works; for example $48$ needs $32 \mid 48$, $55$ needs $25\mid55$, $99$ needs $81\mid99$, all false. Meanwhile $36 = 2\times 18$ works.

**Answer: (C) 36**

ukmt-jmc-2023-05.title: Round the time
ukmt-jmc-2023-05.body:
Speed $=$ distance $\div$ time. The time $19.65$ s is about $20$ s, so the speed is about $100\div20 = 5$ m/s.

**Answer: (E) 5 m/s**

ukmt-jmc-2023-05.title: Check the options
ukmt-jmc-2023-05.body:
At $2.5$ m/s Jumpy would need $100\div2.5 = 40$ s, far too slow; at $5$ m/s he needs $20$ s, which is close to $19.65$ s.

**Answer: (E) 5 m/s**

ukmt-jmc-2023-06.title: Fill in the square
ukmt-jmc-2023-06.body:
Call the missing numbers: $p$ (top middle), $q$ (left middle), $r$ (bottom left), $s$ (bottom right), $t$ (right middle); bottom middle is $29$.
- Top side: $13+p+23 = 43$, so $p = 7$.
- Bottom side: $r+29+s = 43$, so $r+s = 14$. Different primes adding to $14$ (not using $7$ twice): $3+11$.
- Left side: $13+q+r = 43$. If $r = 3$, $q = 27$, not prime. So $r = 11$, $q = 19$, and $s = 3$.
- Right side: $23+t+3 = 43$, so $t = 17$.

The missing primes are $7, 19, 11, 3, 17$ with sum $57$.

**Answer: (D) 57**

ukmt-jmc-2023-06.title: Add the four sides
ukmt-jmc-2023-06.body:
Adding the four side totals counts every middle circle once and every corner twice: $4\times43 = 172 = (\text{all eight}) + (\text{four corners})$. The corners are $13, 23, r, s$ with $r+s = 43-29 = 14$, so the corners total $50$. Then all eight total $172-50 = 122$, and the five missing ones total $122-13-23-29 = 57$.

**Answer: (D) 57**

ukmt-jmc-2023-07.title: Find both numbers
ukmt-jmc-2023-07.body:
The largest two-digit multiple of $2$ is $98$. The smallest three-digit multiple of $3$ is $102$ (since $100$ and $101$ are not multiples of $3$). The difference is $102-98 = 4$.

**Answer: (B) 4**

ukmt-jmc-2023-07.title: Count from 100
ukmt-jmc-2023-07.body:
$98$ is $2$ below $100$ and $102$ is $2$ above $100$, so they differ by $2+2 = 4$.

**Answer: (B) 4**

ukmt-jmc-2023-08.title: Work them out
ukmt-jmc-2023-08.body:
The six numbers are $1, 5, 13, 25, 41, 61$. Of these, $1$ is not prime (by definition) and $25 = 5\times5$ is not prime. The other four, $5, 13, 41, 61$, are prime.

**Answer: (D) 4**

ukmt-jmc-2023-08.title: Spot the pattern
ukmt-jmc-2023-08.body:
$n^2+(n+1)^2$ is always odd. Going up, the numbers increase by $4, 8, 12, 16, 20$: $1, 5, 13, 25, 41, 61$. Checking each for small factors ($3, 5, 7$) shows exactly $1$ and $25$ are not prime, leaving $4$ primes.

**Answer: (D) 4**

ukmt-jmc-2023-09.title: Equal base angles
ukmt-jmc-2023-09.body:
Because $LM = LN$, the base angles at $M$ and $N$ are equal: $2x+8 = 3x-20$, so $x = 28$. Each base angle is $2\times28+8 = 64^\circ$.

The angles of a triangle add to $180^\circ$: $4y-8 = 180-64-64 = 52$, so $4y = 60$ and $y = 15$.

**Answer: (A) 15**

ukmt-jmc-2023-09.title: Try the options
ukmt-jmc-2023-09.body:
The base angles are $64^\circ$ each (from $2x+8 = 3x-20$), so the top angle is $52^\circ$. Now test: $y = 15$ gives $4\times15-8 = 52$. ✓

**Answer: (A) 15**

ukmt-jmc-2023-10.title: Find the height, then subtract the notch
ukmt-jmc-2023-10.body:
The shape is an $18$ cm wide rectangle with a $6$ cm wide notch cut out of the top-left corner. Its perimeter is the same as that of the full rectangle (the notch just moves edges around). If the height is $h$, then $2(18+h) = 60$, so $h = 12$.

The notch is $6$ cm wide and $12-8 = 4$ cm tall. The area is $18\times12 - 6\times4 = 216-24 = 192$ cm$^2$.

**Answer: (A) 192**

ukmt-jmc-2023-10.title: Split into two rectangles
ukmt-jmc-2023-10.body:
With height $12$ (from the perimeter, as above), split the shape by a vertical line $6$ cm from the left: a left part $6\times8 = 48$ and a right part $12\times12 = 144$. Total $48+144 = 192$ cm$^2$.

**Answer: (A) 192**

ukmt-jmc-2023-11.title: Count each round
ukmt-jmc-2023-11.body:
- First use: $120$ bags make $120$ cups.
- Second use: two bags per cup, so $120\div2 = 60$ cups.
- Third use: four bags per cup, so $120\div4 = 30$ cups.

Total: $120+60+30 = 210$ cups.

**Answer: (C) 210**

ukmt-jmc-2023-11.title: Per bag
ukmt-jmc-2023-11.body:
Each bag gives $1 + \frac12 + \frac14 = \frac74$ of a cup. So $120$ bags give $120\times\frac74 = 210$ cups (and $120$ divides evenly by $2$ and $4$, so nothing is wasted).

**Answer: (C) 210**

ukmt-jmc-2023-12.title: Find the speed
ukmt-jmc-2023-12.body:
From 1:50 pm to 2:10 pm (20 minutes) he went $210-150 = 60$ cm, which is $3$ cm per minute. The first $150$ cm took $150\div3 = 50$ minutes, so he started 50 minutes before 1:50 pm, at 1:00 pm.

**Answer: (E) 1 pm**

ukmt-jmc-2023-12.title: Work backwards in 20-minute steps
ukmt-jmc-2023-12.body:
Every 20 minutes he covers $60$ cm. Going back from 1:50 pm (150 cm): 1:30 pm $\to 90$ cm, 1:10 pm $\to 30$ cm. The last $30$ cm takes half of 20 minutes, i.e. 10 minutes, so he started at 1:00 pm.

**Answer: (E) 1 pm**

ukmt-jmc-2023-13.title: Look at a side of the outer square
ukmt-jmc-2023-13.body:
The outer square has area $64$ cm$^2$, so its side is $8$ cm. Each side of the outer square is made of the long side of one rectangle plus the short side of another, so length $+$ width $= 8$ cm. The perimeter of a rectangle is $2\times8 = 16$ cm.

**Answer: (D) 16 cm**

ukmt-jmc-2023-13.title: Find the actual sizes
ukmt-jmc-2023-13.body:
Let the rectangles be $a$ by $b$ with $a > b$. Then $a+b = 8$ and the inner square has side $a-b = \sqrt{20}$. (The individual sizes are not nice numbers, but we don't need them.) The perimeter is $2(a+b) = 16$ cm; the inner area of $20$ cm$^2$ was not needed.

**Answer: (D) 16 cm**

ukmt-jmc-2023-14.title: Column by column
ukmt-jmc-2023-14.body:
**Units:** $x+x+x = 3x$ ends in $7$, so $3x = 27$ and $x = 9$, carrying $2$.

**Tens:** $2+7+y+y$ must end in $x = 9$, so $2y+9$ ends in $9$: $y = 0$ or $y = 5$.

**Hundreds:** if $y = 0$ there is no carry and $7+6+0 = 13$, but we need the answer to start $19\ldots$. If $y = 5$ the tens give $19$, carry $1$, and the hundreds give $1+7+6+5 = 19$. ✓

So $x = 9$, $y = 5$, and $779+659+559 = 1997$. Then $x+y = 14$.

**Answer: (E) 14**

ukmt-jmc-2023-14.title: Write it as one equation
ukmt-jmc-2023-14.body:
The sum is $(770+x)+(600+10y+x)+(110y+x) = 1370+120y+3x$, and this equals $1007+110x$. So $363+120y = 107x$. Trying digits $x$: only $x = 9$ gives $107x-363 = 600 = 120\times5$, so $y = 5$ and $x+y = 14$.

**Answer: (E) 14**

ukmt-jmc-2023-15.title: Work out the journey time
ukmt-jmc-2023-15.body:
From 17:48 to 18:00 is 12 minutes, and then 25 more minutes to 18:25, so the scheduled journey is 37 minutes. The actual journey took $2\times37 = 74$ minutes $= 1$ h $14$ min. The train left at 17:52, so it arrived at $17{:}52 + 1{:}14 = 19{:}06$.

**Answer: (B) 19:06**

ukmt-jmc-2023-15.title: Add on in steps
ukmt-jmc-2023-15.body:
Leaving at 17:52, the first 37 minutes take us to 18:29 (the scheduled arrival plus 4 minutes). Another 37 minutes: 18:29 $\to$ 19:06.

**Answer: (B) 19:06**

ukmt-jmc-2023-16.title: Digit sum must be 22
ukmt-jmc-2023-16.body:
Two-digit multiples of $11$ with non-zero digits are $11, 22, \ldots, 99$. So the PIN looks like $aabb$, with digit sum $2a+2b$, which is even. It is at most $36$, and it must be a multiple of $11$: the only even multiple of $11$ between $4$ and $36$ is $22$. So $a+b = 11$.

The pairs are $(a, b) = (2,9), (3,8), (4,7), (5,6), (6,5), (7,4), (8,3), (9,2)$: eight PINs, e.g. $2299, 3388, \ldots, 9922$.

**Answer: (D) 8**

ukmt-jmc-2023-16.title: List them
ukmt-jmc-2023-16.body:
For each first block $aa$ we need a second block $bb$ with $2(a+b)$ a multiple of $11$, i.e. $a+b = 11$. For $a = 1$ we'd need $b = 10$, impossible; for $a = 2,\ldots,9$ there is exactly one $b$. That gives $8$ PINs.

**Answer: (D) 8**

ukmt-jmc-2023-17.title: Compare with 1
ukmt-jmc-2023-17.body:
- $q-p < q < 1$.
- $p-q$ is negative.
- $\frac{p+q}{2}$ is the average of two numbers less than $1$, so it is less than $1$.
- $\frac pq < 1$ since $p < q$.
- $\frac qp > 1$ since $q > p$.

Only $\frac qp$ is bigger than $1$, so it is the largest.

**Answer: (E) $\frac qp$**

ukmt-jmc-2023-17.title: Try numbers
ukmt-jmc-2023-17.body:
Take $p = \frac14$, $q = \frac12$. Then the expressions are $\frac14, -\frac14, \frac38, \frac12, 2$. The largest is $\frac qp$. (The reasoning in the other solution shows this always happens.)

**Answer: (E) $\frac qp$**

ukmt-jmc-2023-18.title: Use the quadrilateral
ukmt-jmc-2023-18.body:
The four lines form a quadrilateral $PQRS$. Three of the marked angles $p, q, r$ are exterior-type angles on straight lines next to interior angles $180-p$, $180-q$, $180-r$, and the fourth, $s$, is a reflex angle with the interior angle $360-s$ at that vertex.

The interior angles add to $360^\circ$:
$$(180-p)+(180-q)+(180-r)+(360-s) = 360,$$
so $p+q+r+s = 540$.

**Answer: (A) $540^\circ$**

ukmt-jmc-2023-18.title: Check with a special case
ukmt-jmc-2023-18.body:
The total does not depend on the exact positions of the lines, so imagine the quadrilateral is a square. Three marked angles would each be $180-90 = 90^\circ$ and the reflex one $360-90 = 270^\circ$, giving $90+90+90+270 = 540^\circ$.

**Answer: (A) $540^\circ$**

ukmt-jmc-2023-19.title: Count by Rangers' goals
ukmt-jmc-2023-19.body:
At half-time Rangers had $r$ goals and Rovers $v$ goals, with $r \le 5$, $v \le 4$. Rangers were never ahead before the final goal, so either the game was already finished in goals ($5$–$4$) or $r \le v$.

- $r = 0$: $v = 0,1,2,3,4$ (5 scores)
- $r = 1$: $v = 1,\ldots,4$ (4)
- $r = 2$: 3; $r = 3$: 2; $r = 4$: $v = 4$ (1)
- plus $5$–$4$ itself (all goals scored before half-time).

Total $5+4+3+2+1+1 = 16$.

**Answer: (D) 16**

ukmt-jmc-2023-19.title: Grid picture
ukmt-jmc-2023-19.body:
Draw a $6\times5$ grid of possible scores $(r, v)$ with $0\le r\le5$, $0\le v\le4$. The allowed ones are those on or below the diagonal $r = v$ (Rangers not ahead): that's $1+2+3+4+5 = 15$ points with $r\le v$, plus the final score $5$–$4$. Total $16$.

**Answer: (D) 16**

ukmt-jmc-2023-20.title: Try the cubes
ukmt-jmc-2023-20.body:
1 Across is a two-digit cube: $27$ or $64$. 2 Across is a two-digit square, so its first digit (the second digit of 1 Down) is $1, 2, 3, 4, 6$ or $8$.
- If 1 Across is $27$, 1 Down is $2\_$: of $21, 22, 23, 24, 26, 28$ only $23$ is prime, so 2 Across is $36$. Digit sum $2+7+3+6 = 18$.
- If 1 Across is $64$, 1 Down is $6\_$: of $61, 62, 63, 64, 66, 68$ only $61$ is prime, so 2 Across is $16$. Digit sum $6+4+1+6 = 17$.

Only $17$ is an option.

**Answer: (A) 17**

ukmt-jmc-2023-20.title: Start from the prime
ukmt-jmc-2023-20.body:
1 Down is a two-digit prime whose first digit starts a cube ($2$ or $6$) and whose second digit starts a square ($1,2,3,4,6,8$). The candidates are $23$ and $61$. These give the grids $\begin{smallmatrix}2&7\\3&6\end{smallmatrix}$ and $\begin{smallmatrix}6&4\\1&6\end{smallmatrix}$, with digit sums $18$ and $17$.

**Answer: (A) 17**

ukmt-jmc-2023-21.title: Use units
ukmt-jmc-2023-21.body:
Let pygmy $= 1$ unit. Then grey $= 2$, white $= 6$, pink $= 24$ units. White minus pygmy is $5$ units $= 20$, so $1$ unit $= 4$. The total is $1+2+6+24 = 33$ units $= 132$.

**Answer: (B) 132**

ukmt-jmc-2023-21.title: Algebra
ukmt-jmc-2023-21.body:
With $y$ pygmy elephants: grey $2y$, white $6y$, pink $24y$. From $6y = y+20$ we get $y = 4$, so there are $4 + 8 + 24 + 96 = 132$ elephants. (Quick check: the total $33y$ must be a multiple of $33$; only $132 = 33\times4$ among the options is.)

**Answer: (B) 132**

ukmt-jmc-2023-22.title: Track the primes 5 and 7
ukmt-jmc-2023-22.body:
Rows (top to bottom) have products $18, 105, 192$; columns (left to right) $56, 180, 36$.

Only the middle row ($105$) and middle column ($180$) are multiples of $5$, so $5$ is in the centre. Only the middle row ($105$) and left column ($56$) are multiples of $7$, so $7$ is middle-left. Then the middle row gives middle-right $= 105\div35 = 3$.

The right column: $3\times(\text{top-right})\times(\text{bottom-right}) = 36$, so those two multiply to $12$: they are $2$ and $6$ (since $3$ is used and $12 = 2\times6$ is the only option left). If top-right were $6$, the top row would need the other two cells to multiply to $3$, i.e. $1$ and $3$ – but $3$ is used. So top-right is $2$ and bottom-right is $6$.

**Answer: (B) 6**

ukmt-jmc-2023-22.title: Complete the grid
ukmt-jmc-2023-22.body:
Continuing, the full grid is
$$\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & 9 & 2\\ 7 & 5 & 3\\ 8 & 4 & 6\end{array}$$
Rows: $18, 105, 192$ ✓; columns: $56, 180, 36$ ✓. (A computer search over all arrangements confirms it is the only one.) The bottom-right number is $6$.

**Answer: (B) 6**

ukmt-jmc-2023-23.title: Angles at the centre
ukmt-jmc-2023-23.body:
The six equal angles at $O$ are each $60^\circ$. Joining $O$ to the vertices splits the pentagon into five congruent isosceles triangles with angle $72^\circ$ at $O$, so $\angle POT = 72^\circ$ and $\angle OTS = \frac{180-72}{2} = 54^\circ$.

$\angle POG$ is two of the $60^\circ$ angles, i.e. $120^\circ$, so $\angle TOG = 120-72 = 48^\circ$.

In triangle $TOG$: $\angle TGO = 180-48-54 = 78^\circ$.

**Answer: (E) $78^\circ$**

ukmt-jmc-2023-23.title: Measure from OH
ukmt-jmc-2023-23.body:
$OH$ is the line of symmetry through $P$, so it is perpendicular to $RS$ and $\angle HOS = 36^\circ$. $\angle HOG = 60^\circ$, so $G$ lies on $ST$ with $\angle SOG = 60-36 = 24^\circ$. In triangle $SOG$, $\angle OSG = 54^\circ$, so $\angle OGS = 180-24-54 = 102^\circ$ and $\angle TGO = 180-102 = 78^\circ$.

**Answer: (E) $78^\circ$**

ukmt-jmc-2023-24.title: Find her birth year
ukmt-jmc-2023-24.body:
"This year" is 2023. If she was born in $20xy$, her age is $23-(10x+y)$ and the digit sum is $2+x+y$. So $2+x+y = 23-10x-y$, i.e. $11x+2y = 21$. The only digit solution is $x = 1$, $y = 5$: born 2015, aged $8 = 2+0+1+5$. ✓

In year $20pq$ she will be $10p+q-15$, and we need $10p+q-15 = 2(2+p+q)$, i.e. $8p-q = 19$, so $p = 3$, $q = 5$: the year 2035, when she is $20 = 2\times(2+0+3+5)$.

**Answer: (E) 2035**

ukmt-jmc-2023-24.title: Check the options
ukmt-jmc-2023-24.body:
Born in 2015 (found as above). Her ages and twice the digit sums:
- 2027: age 12, $2\times11 = 22$
- 2029: age 14, $2\times13 = 26$
- 2031: age 16, $2\times6 = 12$
- 2033: age 18, $2\times8 = 16$
- 2035: age 20, $2\times10 = 20$ ✓

**Answer: (E) 2035**

ukmt-jmc-2023-25.title: Work backwards
ukmt-jmc-2023-25.body:
The neighbour took everything that was left, say $z$ spoons, and this was 8 more than a third of $z$: $z = \frac z3 + 8$, so $\frac{2z}{3} = 8$ and $z = 12$.

Before the son: if $y$ were left, the son took $\frac y3+8$ and left $\frac{2y}{3}-8 = 12$, so $y = 30$.

At the start: $\frac{2x}{3}-8 = 30$, so $x = 57$. The digit sum is $5+7 = 12$.

**Answer: (B) 12**

ukmt-jmc-2023-25.title: Reverse the operations
ukmt-jmc-2023-25.body:
Each gift turns a pile $N$ into $\frac23N - 8$. To undo it: add $8$, then multiply by $\frac32$. Starting from $0$ spoons at the end: $0\to12\to30\to57$. Check: daughter gets $19+8 = 27$, leaving $30$; son gets $10+8 = 18$, leaving $12$; neighbour gets $4+8 = 12$. ✓ The digit sum of $57$ is $12$.

**Answer: (B) 12**
